questions.title: ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in SQL Server. If two products are tied for the highest price, what number does each function give the row right after them?
questions.modelAnswer: All three are ranking window functions used with OVER(ORDER BY ...), and all three number rows based on the order you specify, but they disagree on what happens with ties. ROW_NUMBER() always assigns a unique, sequential integer to every row, even when two rows are tied on the ORDER BY column -- one of the tied rows arbitrarily gets the lower number. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but then skips ahead by the size of the tie: if two rows tie for rank 1, the next distinct row gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() is really counting 'how many rows came before or tied with me, plus one.' DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but the next distinct value gets the very next integer with no gap -- it's counting distinct values, not rows. So for two products tied for the most expensive: ROW_NUMBER gives them 1 and 2 (arbitrarily), RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 3, and DENSE_RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 2.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with a concrete example because the difference only shows up when there's a tie. Say I'm ranking products by ListPrice and two products are tied for the top price. ROW_NUMBER() doesn't know about ties at all -- it just hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, so the two tied products arbitrarily get 1 and 2. RANK() respects the tie -- both get rank 1 -- but it still 'reserves' a slot for each of them, so the next product down is rank 3, not 2. DENSE_RANK() is the one that feels most natural for something like a pricing tier: both tied products get 1, and the next distinct price is simply 2, no gap. In practice I reach for ROW_NUMBER() constantly for deduplication -- partition by the natural key, order by something like an ID, and anything with RowNum greater than 1 is a duplicate I can delete. I reach for RANK() when ties should genuinely cost a position, like a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for 2nd really does mean nobody is 3rd. And I reach for DENSE_RANK() when I just want the next distinct tier number and don't want gaps confusing anyone reading the report.
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- If two products tie for the top ListPrice:
-- RowNum:     1, 2, 3, 4...  (ties broken arbitrarily)
-- Rank_:      1, 1, 3, 4...  (skips to 3 after the tie)
-- DenseRank_: 1, 1, 2, 3...  (no gap after the tie)
commonMistakes: Saying ROW_NUMBER() can produce duplicate numbers for ties (it never can -- it's always unique)
Mixing up which function skips numbers after a tie (it's RANK, not DENSE_RANK)
Forgetting that ROW_NUMBER() requires ORDER BY inside OVER() -- without it, row order is undefined
Not realizing all three still need PARTITION BY to restart numbering per group
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, ties broken arbitrarily
RANK() gives ties the same number and skips ahead by the tie size afterward
DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same number with no gap for the next distinct value
Choice depends on whether the business question treats a tie as 'costing' a rank

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes ROW_NUMBER's uniqueness behavior
Correctly describes RANK's gap-after-tie behavior
Correctly describes DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over another

questions.title: Top-2-per-group with a window function
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns the two highest-priced products in each color, without using a correlated subquery.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic way to solve 'top N per group' in T-SQL is PARTITION BY plus ROW_NUMBER(), wrapped in a CTE so the ranking column can be filtered afterward. PARTITION BY Color restarts the numbering at 1 for each color, and ORDER BY ListPrice DESC makes 1 the most expensive product in that color. You can't filter directly on ROW_NUMBER() in the same SELECT's WHERE clause because window functions are logically evaluated after WHERE -- that's why the CTE (or a subquery) is necessary.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'top N per group' problem, and the pattern I reach for every time is a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the grouping column. I avoid a correlated subquery with TOP 2 inside it because that approach re-executes once per outer row and doesn't scale well. Instead, I compute the rank once in a CTE, then just filter WHERE RankInColor <= 2 in the outer query. The one gotcha I always mention out loud in an interview: you cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 2 directly in the same SELECT, because the WHERE clause is logically evaluated before window functions are computed -- that's exactly why the CTE wrapper is required, not just a style preference.
questions.example:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Color ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RankInColor
    FROM Production.Product
)
SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice
FROM Ranked
WHERE RankInColor <= 2
ORDER BY Color, RankInColor;
-- The CTE is required because ROW_NUMBER() can't be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
commonMistakes: Trying to filter WHERE ROW_NUMBER() <= 2 directly in the same SELECT (not legal -- window functions evaluate after WHERE)
Forgetting PARTITION BY and ranking across the whole table instead of per color
Using TOP 2 with a correlated subquery per group, which is correct but far less efficient on large tables
Omitting ORDER BY inside OVER(), which leaves 'top' undefined
keyPoints: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking per group (per color here)
A CTE or subquery is required to filter on the window function's result
ORDER BY DESC inside OVER() makes rank 1 the highest price
This pattern generalizes to any 'top N per group' business question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses ROW_NUMBER() with correct PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
Wraps it in a CTE/subquery to filter correctly
Query is syntactically valid and returns exactly 2 rows per color
Explains why filtering can't happen in the same SELECT's WHERE clause

questions.title: What MERGE actually does
questions.prompt: A coworker wants to sync a staging table into a permanent dimension table using separate UPDATE, INSERT, and DELETE statements. Explain what the MERGE statement does instead, and what each of its three WHEN clauses corresponds to.
questions.modelAnswer: MERGE combines insert, update, and delete logic into a single statement based on a join between a target table and a source. You join target and source ON some matching key, then handle three scenarios: WHEN MATCHED runs when a row exists in both target and source -- typically an UPDATE, equivalent to an INNER JOIN match. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET runs when a row exists in source but not target -- typically an INSERT, equivalent to the unmatched side of a LEFT JOIN from source. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE runs when a row exists in target but not source -- typically a DELETE (or an update to mark it inactive), equivalent to the unmatched side of a LEFT JOIN from target. All of this happens in one atomic statement instead of three separate ones with separate matching logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them MERGE is exactly the three statements they're already writing, just unified around one join so you don't have to repeat the matching logic three times and risk it drifting out of sync between statements. I always explain it by mapping it back to joins, because that's the mental model people already have: WHEN MATCHED is your INNER JOIN case -- the row is in both places, so update it. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET is the new rows showing up in the source that haven't landed in the target yet -- insert them. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is rows that used to be in the target but have disappeared from the source -- that's your delete, or sometimes a soft-delete flag instead. For warehouse loads specifically, I like MERGE because the whole sync is one atomic operation -- there's no window where the target is left half-updated if something fails partway through.
questions.example:
MERGE Production.Product AS target
USING StagingProduct AS source
    ON target.ProductID = source.ProductID
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET target.ListPrice = source.ListPrice
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (ProductID, Name, ListPrice)
    VALUES (source.ProductID, source.Name, source.ListPrice)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN
    DELETE;
-- One atomic statement instead of three separate UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE statements.
commonMistakes: Confusing WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET (new rows to insert) with WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE (stale rows to delete)
Forgetting MERGE requires a semicolon terminator in SQL Server
Not realizing MERGE is still just a join under the hood -- overcomplicating the explanation
Using MERGE for a simple single-table update when a plain UPDATE would be simpler and clearer
keyPoints: MERGE unifies insert, update, and delete around one source-to-target join
WHEN MATCHED = INNER JOIN case (update)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET = new row in source (insert)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE = row missing from source (delete)
The whole sync happens in one atomic statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what MERGE replaces and why it's useful
Correctly maps all three WHEN clauses to their scenarios
Connects the WHEN clauses to join semantics (INNER/LEFT JOIN unmatched sides)

questions.title: Write a MERGE to sync a staging table into a dimension
questions.prompt: Write a MERGE statement that syncs a StagingCustomer table into a DimCustomer table: update existing customers' names, insert new customers, and leave customers who disappeared from staging alone (do not delete them).
questions.modelAnswer: This requires only two of MERGE's three WHEN clauses -- WHEN MATCHED for updates and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET for inserts -- and deliberately omitting WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, since the requirement is to leave disappeared customers untouched rather than deleting them. Omitting a WHEN clause simply means MERGE does nothing for that scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key thing here is recognizing that MERGE's three WHEN clauses are each optional -- you only write the ones you need. Since the requirement explicitly says not to delete customers who vanish from staging, I just don't write a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause at all. MERGE doesn't require all three; leaving one out means that scenario simply does nothing, which is exactly the 'leave them alone' behavior requested. This comes up constantly in dimension loads -- you often want to sync new and changed records without ever purging history just because a source feed temporarily dropped a row.
questions.example:
MERGE DimCustomer AS target
USING StagingCustomer AS source
    ON target.CustomerID = source.CustomerID
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET target.CustomerName = source.CustomerName
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (CustomerID, CustomerName)
    VALUES (source.CustomerID, source.CustomerName);
-- No WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause -- customers missing from staging are left untouched.
commonMistakes: Adding a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE clause when the requirement explicitly says not to delete
Forgetting the trailing semicolon, which SQL Server requires after MERGE
Updating columns that didn't change, instead of only the ones the requirement calls for (CustomerName)
Joining on the wrong key (e.g. a surrogate key that doesn't exist yet in staging) instead of the natural/business key
keyPoints: WHEN clauses in MERGE are each optional -- omit the ones you don't need
Omitting WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE means disappeared rows are left alone, not deleted
Join on the business/natural key that staging and the dimension share
MERGE still requires a terminating semicolon in SQL Server

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct WHEN MATCHED update logic
Correct WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET insert logic
Correctly omits any delete logic per the requirement
Valid, runnable MERGE syntax with correct join predicate

questions.title: Transactions: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
questions.prompt: Explain what a transaction is in SQL Server, what COMMIT does that running the statements without a transaction wouldn't, and what exactly ROLLBACK undoes.
questions.modelAnswer: A transaction groups one or more statements into a single all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION marks the start of that group. Until COMMIT runs, the changes are provisional -- visible in the current session but not yet permanently saved, and still subject to being undone. COMMIT TRANSACTION makes every change inside the group permanent, all at once. ROLLBACK TRANSACTION undoes every change made since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION, as if none of it had ever happened. The reason this matters: a multi-step change (like moving stock from one location to another with two separate UPDATE statements) can fail halfway through if run as two independent statements, leaving the data in an inconsistent state. Wrapping both statements in a transaction guarantees either both succeed or neither does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I usually explain this with the classic example: moving inventory from warehouse A to warehouse B is really two UPDATEs -- subtract from A, add to B. If I just run those as two separate statements and the second one fails, I've got stock that's vanished into nowhere. A transaction fixes that by treating both statements as one all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION starts the clock; until I COMMIT, those changes are provisional -- I can see them in my own session, but they're not durably saved and SQL Server can still throw them away. COMMIT makes them permanent. ROLLBACK is the safety net -- if something goes wrong partway through, it undoes everything back to the BEGIN, cleanly, as if I'd never run anything at all. The discipline I bring to it professionally is keeping transactions as short as possible, because every lock held inside one is held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK runs.
commonMistakes: Thinking changes inside a transaction are already permanent before COMMIT runs
Forgetting that ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN TRANSACTION, not just the most recent statement
Leaving a transaction open for a long time, holding locks and blocking other users unnecessarily
Not pairing every BEGIN TRANSACTION with a guaranteed COMMIT or ROLLBACK, even on the error path
keyPoints: A transaction is an all-or-nothing group of statements
Changes are provisional until COMMIT makes them permanent
ROLLBACK undoes everything since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION
Transactions exist to prevent partial, inconsistent multi-step changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a transaction groups together
Correctly explains what COMMIT does and the provisional state before it
Correctly explains the scope of what ROLLBACK undoes
Gives a realistic scenario showing why this matters

questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock
Correctly explains SQL Server's automatic deadlock resolution
Proposes consistent table access order as a concrete fix
Proposes shortening transactions as a concrete fix

questions.title: Choosing a clustering key for a new fact-staging table
questions.prompt: You're designing a new staging table that will be loaded nightly and queried immediately afterward by ProductID ranges. A table can have only one clustered index. Explain the difference between a clustered and nonclustered index, and what makes a good choice of clustering key.
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order rows are stored in on disk -- which is exactly why a table can have only one: data can only be physically sorted one way. A nonclustered index is a separate structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the actual row, and a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through the clustering key is fastest, since SQL Server navigates directly to the physical location; looking up through a nonclustered index takes one extra step -- find the index entry, then follow the pointer back to the row. A good clustering key is narrow (a small data type, since every nonclustered index secretly stores the clustering key as its row pointer), unique (no ambiguity about physical order), and ever-increasing (so new rows append at the end instead of forcing existing rows to physically shuffle). Given the staging table is loaded nightly and then range-queried by ProductID, an ever-increasing identity key for the clustered index, with a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries, is the more defensible design than clustering directly on ProductID.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate decisions. First: what should the table's physical row order be -- that's the clustered index, and I only get one shot at it. Second: what other lookup patterns do I need to support cheaply -- that's where nonclustered indexes come in, and I can have several. For a staging table that's loaded nightly, I actually lean toward an ever-increasing identity column as the clustering key rather than ProductID directly, even though ProductID is the column people will query by. The reason is load performance: an ever-increasing key means new rows always append at the end of the physical order, so the nightly load doesn't cause page splits from inserting into the middle of existing data. Then I add a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries -- yes, that costs one extra pointer-following step per lookup compared to clustering directly on ProductID, but it's a much smaller cost than the load-time page-splitting I'd get from clustering on a column that isn't naturally ordered or unique.
commonMistakes: Assuming more indexes are always better without considering the nightly load's insert cost
Choosing a wide, non-unique column as the clustering key, which bloats every nonclustered index that secretly carries it as a pointer
Forgetting a table can have only one clustered index, and trying to 'cluster' on two different columns
Not connecting the ever-increasing key recommendation to the specific nightly-load write pattern described in the scenario
keyPoints: Clustered index = physical row order, one per table
Nonclustered index = separate structure with a pointer back to the row, many allowed
Good clustering key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing
Design choice should weigh load (insert) pattern against query (read) pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the clustered vs. nonclustered distinction
Correctly lists the three traits of a good clustering key
Applies the tradeoff to the specific nightly-load scenario given
Recommends a nonclustered index to support the ProductID range queries

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the predicate as non-SARGable and explains why
Correctly explains why this matters more as the table grows
Provides a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Rewrite correctly handles the full year's date range without off-by-one errors

questions.title: Temp table, table variable, or CTE?
questions.prompt: You need to hold an intermediate result set of about 500,000 rows, reuse it across three separate statements in a stored procedure, and would benefit from adding your own index to it. Which of #temp table, @table variable, or CTE would you choose, and why would the other two be worse choices here?
questions.modelAnswer: A #temp table is the right choice. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, so SQL Server maintains real statistics on it (row counts), which lets the optimizer build a much smarter plan for a large result set, and you can explicitly add your own indexes to it. A table variable would be the wrong choice here: it also lives in tempdb, but historically has no maintained statistics, so on older compatibility levels the optimizer may assume just one row and badly under-allocate resources for 500,000 rows -- and while you can add inline PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraints, you can't add arbitrary indexes the way you can on a #temp table. A CTE would also be the wrong choice: it isn't physically stored at all -- it's inlined into the query -- so referencing it in three separate statements could mean SQL Server re-runs its underlying query multiple times, and you can't add an index to something that was never materialized.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given the three constraints in the question -- large row count, reused across multiple statements, and wanting an index -- a #temp table wins on all three. The decision rule I use: CTEs are for one-time readability or recursion, not for reuse -- a CTE doesn't store anything, it's re-inlined at every reference, so touching it from three separate statements risks the underlying query running three separate times. Table variables are for small result sets inside a procedure where I want to avoid plan recompiles -- but historically they carry no real statistics, so the optimizer can badly misjudge a large one. A #temp table is the one option that's physically stored with real statistics the optimizer can use, and the only one of the three where I can explicitly add an index after the fact. For 500,000 rows reused three times, I'm reaching for #temp every time.
commonMistakes: Choosing a CTE for something reused across multiple statements, not realizing it may re-run its query each time
Choosing a table variable for a large result set, assuming it always performs the same as a temp table
Not mentioning that #temp tables maintain real statistics while table variables historically don't
Forgetting that CTEs can't be indexed at all, since nothing is actually materialized
keyPoints: #Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and can be indexed
Table variables historically lack statistics, risking a poor plan on large sets
CTEs are inlined, not stored, and may re-execute their query on every reference
Choice depends on size, reuse, and whether an index is needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses the #temp table for this scenario
Correctly explains why a table variable would be worse here
Correctly explains why a CTE would be worse here

questions.title: Raising a custom business-rule error
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that checks whether a discount percentage exceeds 50% and, if so, raises a custom error using the modern recommended syntax. Then show how you would log an error inside a CATCH block and still let it propagate to the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error, taking an error number, a message, and a state, and raising it exactly as if SQL Server had generated it itself. For a business rule like a discount cap, you check the condition and THROW a custom error if it's violated. To log an error and still propagate it, use THROW with no arguments inside a CATCH block -- it re-raises the exact error that was just caught, unmodified, after whatever logging or cleanup logic runs first. RAISERROR is the older syntax, still common in existing code, with a different argument shape (message, severity, state) -- recognize it, but prefer THROW for new code.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the business rule check itself, I'd write a simple IF that tests the discount, and THROW a custom error number with a clear message if it's violated -- that's the modern, recommended way, and it's a one-liner. The more interesting half of this question is re-throwing from a CATCH block, because that's a pattern people often get wrong: they either swallow the error silently after logging it, or they try to reconstruct it with a new THROW statement and lose the original error details. The clean way is TRY/CATCH around the risky operation, log whatever you need to inside CATCH, and then just write THROW with no arguments -- that re-raises the exact error that was caught, unmodified, so the caller still sees the real failure instead of a sanitized stand-in.
questions.example:
-- Business rule check
IF @DiscountPercent > 50
    THROW 50000, 'Discount cannot exceed 50 percent.', 1;

-- Logging then re-throwing the original error
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Sales.SpecialOffer SET DiscountPct = @DiscountPercent WHERE SpecialOfferID = @ID;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    INSERT INTO ErrorLog (ErrorMessage, LoggedAt) VALUES (ERROR_MESSAGE(), GETDATE());
    THROW; -- re-raises the exact caught error, unmodified
END CATCH
commonMistakes: Using RAISERROR for new code instead of the modern, recommended THROW
Writing a new THROW statement inside CATCH instead of bare THROW, which loses the original error's details
Forgetting THROW's argument order is (error number, message, state) -- a different shape than RAISERROR's
Swallowing the error entirely after logging it, instead of re-throwing so the caller knows it failed
keyPoints: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error
Bare THROW inside CATCH re-raises the exact original error
RAISERROR is the older syntax, still seen in legacy code
Logging an error doesn't have to mean swallowing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses THROW to raise a custom business-rule error
Correctly uses TRY/CATCH with bare THROW to re-raise after logging
Explains the difference between THROW and RAISERROR
Code is syntactically valid T-SQL

questions.title: Diagnosing a performance problem under deadline pressure
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to track down a slow query or a failing ETL job under time pressure. How did you approach diagnosing it, and how did you communicate progress to whoever was waiting on the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer uses a structured approach: first isolate the actual symptom (which query, which job step, when it started happening versus when it was fine), then form a specific hypothesis before changing anything (e.g. 'the predicate on OrderDate looks non-SARGable' or 'this package step has no checkpoint so every retry starts from scratch'), test that hypothesis cheaply (check the execution plan, check the job history), and only then apply a fix. Equally important under deadline pressure is proactive, specific communication -- not 'still looking into it' every hour, but 'I've confirmed it's a missing index on X, applying the fix now, expect it resolved in 15 minutes' -- so stakeholders can make their own decisions about what to do in the meantime.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a real situation concretely: what broke, how I noticed, and the actual diagnostic steps I took in order -- not jumping straight to a fix before confirming the cause. I'd emphasize that I checked the obvious things first (recent changes, data volume growth, whether this ever worked) before assuming something exotic was wrong, and that I gave the person waiting on it a clear, specific update rather than vague reassurance -- something like 'I've narrowed it to a non-SARGable predicate in the nightly load query, testing the fix now, should have it confirmed within the hour' instead of just 'working on it.' I'd close with what I changed afterward so it wouldn't happen again -- a monitoring alert, a code review checklist item -- because recovering from one incident well is good, but preventing the repeat is what actually builds trust with the team.
commonMistakes: Describing only the technical fix with no mention of how the situation was communicated under pressure
Jumping to 'I just reindexed everything' without explaining how the root cause was actually diagnosed
Giving a vague, non-specific story instead of a real situation with a concrete before/after
Leaving out what changed afterward to prevent the same issue recurring

questions.title: SSIS event handlers and OnError bubbling
questions.prompt: A package has a Sequence container with three Execute SQL tasks inside it. One of the tasks fails but has no OnError event handler of its own. Explain where that OnError event goes, and why a single package-level OnError handler is often enough to catch failures anywhere in the package.
questions.modelAnswer: Every executable in SSIS -- the package itself, a container, or a task -- raises events as it runs, including OnError the moment something goes wrong. An event handler is a workflow you build on the Event Handlers tab, scoped to a specific executable and a specific event, that runs in response. If a task raises OnError and that task has no OnError handler of its own, the event doesn't disappear -- it bubbles up to the next container in the hierarchy. In this scenario: the failing task escalates to the Sequence container; if the Sequence container also has no OnError handler, it escalates further to the package itself. If the package has an OnError handler, that's where it finally runs. This is exactly why one package-level OnError handler is often sufficient to catch failures anywhere in a package, without wiring an individual handler onto every single task.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as escalation, because that's the mental model that makes it click. Every task, container, and the package itself can raise an OnError event, and an event handler is just a second, hidden control flow scoped to one specific executable and one specific event -- built with the same Toolbox, same tasks, same design surface as regular Control Flow. If the failing Execute SQL task has no handler of its own, the event doesn't vanish -- it bubbles up one level, to the Sequence container. If the Sequence container doesn't have a handler either, it keeps bubbling, all the way up to the package. So in practice, I almost never wire an OnError handler onto every single task -- I put one OnError handler at the package level, drop a Send Mail task on it, and that one handler catches failures from anywhere in the package tree, because anything unhandled downstream escalates straight to it.

Thinking you need to wire an OnError handler onto every single task individually
Confusing the Event Handlers tab with a dialog box or checkbox, rather than a full design surface
Not realizing the Event Handlers tab uses the same Toolbox and containers as regular Control Flow

One package-level OnError handler is often enough to catch failures anywhere

questions.title: A package fails halfway through a five-task load
questions.prompt: A package runs five Bulk Insert tasks in sequence, each loading a different dimension table. The fourth one fails due to a bad connection. Without any restart strategy, fixing the connection means re-running all five tasks from scratch. Explain how checkpoints solve this, the three package properties involved, and one real limitation of checkpoint restart granularity.
questions.modelAnswer: SSIS writes progress information to a checkpoint file as the package runs; if the package fails, that file records exactly how far it got, and rerunning the package picks up from the point of failure instead of the beginning. Three package properties turn this on: SaveCheckpoints (set to True to actually write the checkpoint file -- the master switch), CheckpointFileName (the file path checkpoint data is written to), and CheckpointUsage (Never / Always / IfExists -- IfExists is the setting used most often, restarting from the checkpoint if the file exists, otherwise starting clean). FailPackageOnFailure must also be set to True on each task or container you want to serve as a restart point, or its failure won't register correctly for checkpoint purposes. The key limitation: a package can only restart at the control flow level -- the task host container is the smallest atomic unit that can be a restart point. You cannot restart partway through a single Data Flow task; if it fails five minutes into a ten-minute load, the whole task reruns from its own beginning. If finer restart granularity matters, the answer is to split the work into multiple smaller Data Flow tasks in Control Flow.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through exactly why re-running from scratch is wasteful here -- tasks one through three already succeeded, so redoing them isn't just slow, it's also risky if any of those loads aren't safely repeatable. Checkpoints fix this by having SSIS write a progress file as it runs, so a rerun can skip what already succeeded and pick up exactly where it failed. Turning it on takes three properties on the package itself: SaveCheckpoints as the master on/off switch, CheckpointFileName for where that file lives, and CheckpointUsage set to IfExists, which is the one I use almost every time -- restart from the checkpoint if it's there, otherwise just run clean. The part people miss is FailPackageOnFailure -- without setting that to True on each task, its failure doesn't actually register as a valid restart point. As for the limitation, this is the one I always flag proactively in an interview: restart only works at the control-flow level, so you can't resume partway through a single Data Flow task -- if a ten-minute data flow dies at minute nine, it reruns the whole ten minutes. If that granularity matters, the fix isn't inside the data flow at all -- it's splitting the work into several smaller Data Flow tasks in Control Flow so each one is cheap to rerun entirely.
commonMistakes: Forgetting FailPackageOnFailure must be set to True for a task to register as a valid restart point
Assuming checkpoints can restart mid-Data-Flow-task, when the real granularity limit is the task host container
Mixing up CheckpointUsage's three settings (Never/Always/IfExists) and when each applies
Not knowing that For Loop and Foreach Loop containers don't checkpoint their individual iterations
keyPoints: Checkpoint file records progress so a rerun resumes from the point of failure

FailPackageOnFailure must be True on a task/container for it to count as a restart point
Restart granularity is limited to the control-flow (task host) level, never mid-Data-Flow-task
Splitting work into smaller Data Flow tasks is the workaround for finer restart granularity

questions.title: Configuring a Lookup for an incremental load
questions.prompt: You're building an incremental load: fact rows carry a ProductID, and you need to tag each incoming row as either 'existing product' or 'new product' by checking it against the Product dimension. Describe how you'd configure a Lookup transformation to do this, including cache mode and how unmatched rows are handled.
questions.modelAnswer: Drop a Lookup transformation into the data flow after the source, pointed at the Product dimension as its reference dataset, joining on ProductID. On the General page, choose a cache mode: Full cache loads the entire Product dimension into memory once before the Lookup runs -- fast per-row lookups, more memory, and the cache reflects a single point in time, which is appropriate here since the dimension is relatively stable during one load. On the Columns page, drag ProductID from Available Input Columns to its match in Available Lookup Columns to build the join. By default, unmatched rows are treated as errors, so on the General page you must explicitly set 'Specify how to handle rows with no matching entries' to 'Redirect rows to no match output.' This gives you two usable outputs: the Match output (existing products) and the No Match output (new products) -- exactly the 'existing vs. new' split the incremental load needs, each routed to its own downstream destination or transformation.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic SSIS incremental-load pattern, so I'd walk through it output by output. The Lookup goes right after the source, joined to the Product dimension on ProductID. For cache mode, I'd default to Full cache unless the dimension is enormous or needs to reflect same-run changes, because it's the fastest option for repeated per-row lookups and the dimension typically isn't changing mid-load. The step people forget is on the General page: by default, a row with no match is treated as an error, not as a legitimate 'this is new' signal -- so I have to explicitly switch that setting to 'Redirect rows to no match output.' Once that's set, the Lookup gives me exactly two outputs to route downstream: Match output, which are rows that already exist in the dimension, and No Match output, which are the new products -- I can send those down a separate path, maybe through a dimension-insert step, before the fact load continues. This exact pattern is also how incremental loads detect new vs. existing rows generally, not just for products.

-- Conceptual SSIS configuration, not T-SQL:
-- 1. Lookup transformation, Connection page -> Product dimension table, join on ProductID
-- 2. General page -> Cache mode: Full cache
-- 3. General page -> 'Specify how to handle rows with no matching entries' -> Redirect rows to no match output
-- 4. Route Lookup Match Output -> existing-product path
-- 5. Route Lookup No Match Output -> new-product path (e.g. insert into dimension first)

questions.title: Lookup transformation cache modes
questions.prompt: Explain the three cache modes available on an SSIS Lookup transformation -- Full cache, Partial cache, and No cache -- and the tradeoff each one makes between performance and data freshness.
questions.modelAnswer: Full cache queries the entire reference dataset once and loads it into memory before the Lookup runs -- fast per-row lookups, but uses more memory and the cache reflects a single point in time. Partial cache caches rows incrementally as they're looked up during execution, caching both matches and non-matches, with least-frequently-used rows evicted once the cache fills up. No cache queries the reference dataset live for every single lookup, with no caching at all -- the slowest option, but always current. Full cache uses an OLE DB connection manager or a Cache connection manager (which lets a prebuilt cache be shared across multiple packages); Partial cache and No cache always query live through an OLE DB connection manager.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of these three modes as a straight line from fastest-but-stalest to slowest-but-freshest. Full cache front-loads the entire reference table into memory before any row flows through -- it's the fastest option for repeated lookups, but the data is frozen at whatever it was when the cache was built, and it costs memory proportional to the reference table's size. No cache is the opposite extreme: every lookup is a live query against the source, so it's always current, but it's the slowest option because there's a round trip per row. Partial cache sits in between -- it caches rows on demand as they're actually looked up, evicting the least-recently-used ones once it fills up, which is a reasonable middle ground when the reference set is too large to fully cache but you still want to avoid re-querying rows you've already seen. In practice, I default to Full cache for relatively small, stable dimension tables, and I'd only reach for No cache if the reference data is genuinely changing mid-run and that freshness actually matters to the business logic.

Assuming No cache is never the right choice, when it's actually correct whenever freshness matters more than speed

Not mentioning the memory cost tradeoff that comes with Full cache
keyPoints: Full cache: entire reference set loaded once, fastest, frozen at one point in time
Partial cache: caches incrementally as rows are looked up, evicts least-used rows
No cache: always queries live, slowest, always current
Choice trades performance against freshness based on reference data volatility

questions.title: Designing an incremental load control flow
questions.prompt: Design the control flow and data flow for an incremental load of a sales fact table from a source system: only new or changed rows should be processed, not a full reload every night. Describe which components you'd use and how they fit together.
questions.modelAnswer: The data flow starts with an OLE DB Source pulling rows from the source system, typically filtered to only rows changed since the last load (using a watermark column like ModifiedDate, or a change-tracking mechanism). A Lookup transformation then checks each incoming row against the existing fact or staging table on its business key, configured to redirect unmatched rows to the No Match output instead of treating them as errors. A Conditional Split (or simply routing the Lookup's two outputs separately) then divides rows into 'new' (Lookup No Match -- route to an insert destination) and 'existing but possibly changed' (Lookup Match -- route to an OLE DB Command or a staging table merged in afterward with a MERGE statement). The control flow wraps this Data Flow task with an Execute SQL Task beforehand to capture the current watermark value, and typically an Execute SQL Task afterward to update the watermark for next time, so each run only picks up what's genuinely new since the last successful load.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe this the way I'd actually build it. First, in Control Flow, an Execute SQL Task reads the last successful watermark value (say, the maximum ModifiedDate already loaded) into a package variable. Then a Data Flow task does the real work: an OLE DB Source query filtered to WHERE ModifiedDate > the watermark variable, so I'm only ever pulling what's changed since last time -- not a full table scan every night. That feeds into a Lookup against the existing fact or staging table on the business key, configured to redirect no-match rows instead of erroring. From there I split into two paths -- new rows (Lookup No Match) go straight to an insert destination, and existing-but-changed rows (Lookup Match) go to an OLE DB Command for a targeted update, or get staged and merged with a MERGE statement afterward, which is often cleaner than row-by-row OLE DB Command updates for larger volumes. Back in Control Flow, after the Data Flow task succeeds, a final Execute SQL Task updates the stored watermark to the maximum ModifiedDate just processed, so the next run picks up exactly where this one left off.

Forgetting to update the watermark value after a successful load, causing the same rows to reprocess every time

Using row-by-row OLE DB Command updates for a very large changed-row volume instead of staging and using MERGE

A Lookup against the existing table identifies which rows are new vs. already present
New and existing rows route to different downstream paths (insert vs. update/merge)
The watermark must be updated after a successful load so the next run doesn't reprocess old rows

questions.title: The Slowly Changing Dimension transformation wizard
questions.prompt: Explain what the SSIS Slowly Changing Dimension transformation does, and how it treats a column marked as a 'Changing attribute' (Type 1) differently from a column marked as an 'Historical attribute' (Type 2).
questions.modelAnswer: The Slowly Changing Dimension transformation is a wizard-driven data flow component that compares incoming source rows against an existing dimension table and automatically generates the outputs needed to apply Type 1 and Type 2 changes, instead of hand-writing that comparison logic. During setup, you map each dimension column to a change type. A column marked as a 'Changing attribute' (Type 1) gets overwritten in place when it changes -- the transformation routes those rows to a 'Changing Attributes Updates Output' that feeds a straightforward update of the existing row, with no history kept. A column marked as an 'Historical attribute' (Type 2) triggers versioning when it changes -- the transformation routes those rows to an 'Historical Attributes Inserts Output,' which is wired to close out the old row (expiring it) and insert a brand-new row representing the new version, preserving the old row as history.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the SCD transformation as a wizard that saves you from hand-coding the comparison logic between incoming source rows and the existing dimension. Walking through the wizard, the key step is marking each dimension column with a change type. Anything marked a 'Changing attribute' is treated as Type 1 -- when that column's value differs from what's already in the dimension, the wizard routes that row to its Changing Attributes Updates Output, which just overwrites the existing row in place, no history. Anything marked an 'Historical attribute' is treated as Type 2 -- when that column changes, the row goes to the Historical Attributes Inserts Output instead, and the wizard wires up the logic to expire the old row and insert a new versioned row, so the history is preserved. In practice I've found the wizard useful for getting a working SCD pattern quickly, but it's also known for being slower on large dimensions than a hand-rolled T-SQL MERGE-based Type 2 pattern, so for bigger warehouses I'll sometimes use the wizard to prototype the logic and then reimplement it as a set-based MERGE for production performance.

Assuming the wizard handles Type 2's surrogate key generation without any additional configuration

questions.title: An OnError handler that isn't catching anything
questions.prompt: A developer builds an OnError event handler on a specific Data Flow task, but a different task in the same package fails and no email alert goes out. Explain the most likely reason, referencing how event handler scoping works.
questions.modelAnswer: An event handler is scoped to a specific executable, chosen in the 'Executable' dropdown on the Event Handlers tab -- in this case, that one Data Flow task, and nothing else. The task that actually failed is a different executable, and since it has no OnError handler of its own, its OnError event bubbles up to the next container above it, not sideways to a handler built on a sibling task. Unless that bubbling path eventually reaches a container or the package itself that does have an OnError handler, the event never triggers the email alert at all. The fix is to move the handler (or add an equivalent one) to a container that's actually an ancestor of the failing task -- most robustly, at the package level, so any unhandled failure anywhere in the tree bubbles all the way up to it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first question I'd ask is: which executable is that OnError handler actually scoped to? Handlers aren't global -- they're built against one specific entry in the Executable dropdown, and this one was built against a Data Flow task that isn't the one that failed. Since the failing task has no handler of its own, its OnError event bubbles upward through its own container hierarchy, not sideways into a handler sitting on an unrelated sibling task. So unless the failing task's ancestors happen to include something with its own OnError handler, the bubbling path dead-ends with nothing listening, and no email ever fires. My fix would be to either add a matching handler to the failing task directly, or -- the more robust move -- delete the narrowly-scoped handler and rebuild it at the package level instead, so it catches bubbled-up failures from anywhere in the package, not just one specific task.

Thinking the handler is broken or misconfigured rather than simply scoped to the wrong executable

Fixing it by duplicating the handler on every task instead of placing one at a shared ancestor or the package level

questions.title: Designing restart strategy across a multi-package ETL run
questions.prompt: You're designing a nightly ETL run of six packages, where package 4 both uses checkpoints for restartability and wraps part of its work in a transaction. What's the risk in combining checkpoints and transactions in the same package, and how would you structure the package to avoid it?
questions.modelAnswer: Checkpoints and transactions can actively fight each other: if a container both uses a transaction and sits within a checkpoint's reach, a restart from the checkpoint file can replay a transaction that already committed successfully the first time, producing duplicated or inconsistent results. Microsoft's own guidance is explicit that using both together in the same package 'could cause unexpected results.' The safer architecture is to keep checkpoints and transactions in separate parts of the package rather than layering one directly on top of the other -- for example, put the transactional logic in a Sequence container that either succeeds completely or is excluded from the checkpoint's restart boundary entirely, and let checkpoint-based restart apply only to the non-transactional steps around it.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those SSIS gotchas that doesn't show up until you hit it in production. The risk is that checkpoints and transactions solve overlapping but different problems -- checkpoints are about 'where do I resume,' and transactions are about 'did this already commit' -- and when they overlap on the same container, a restart can resume at a point where the transaction had already committed the first time, so the package replays work that's already durably saved, which can mean double-inserts or other inconsistent results. Microsoft's own docs are blunt that combining the two in the same package 'could cause unexpected results,' so I take that as a hard design constraint, not a suggestion. My approach would be to physically separate them in the package: keep the transactional logic self-contained in its own Sequence container, and design the checkpoint boundaries so that container is either entirely inside or entirely outside any restart point -- never split in a way where a restart could land in the middle of work the transaction already committed.

Not recognizing that a restart replaying an already-committed transaction is the specific failure mode

Treating this as a minor edge case rather than a real production risk Microsoft explicitly warns about

questions.title: How cascading parameters actually work
questions.prompt: Explain how a three-level cascading parameter setup (Country, then State, then City) works in SSRS. Where does the actual filtering logic live, and why must the parameters appear in a specific order?
questions.modelAnswer: A cascading parameter setup isn't a single property you flip on -- it's a chain of separate datasets, each one filtered by the parameter chosen before it. There's no one dialog showing the whole chain; it's spread across each dataset's own Filters tab. The State dataset's Filters tab has an Expression (the column being tested), an Operator, and a Value of [@CountryParameter] -- the current value of the Country parameter. The City dataset's Filters tab similarly references [@StateParameter]. Three parameters, three datasets, three filters, each pointed at the parameter one level up. Order matters because the order parameters appear under the Parameters node in the Report Data pane is the order the reader is prompted for them at runtime -- and because the State dataset's filter references the Country parameter's value, Country must be prompted (and therefore listed) before State, and State before City. A parameter can't reference a value that hasn't been chosen yet.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I always clarify first is that 'cascading parameters' isn't one setting -- it's an illusion created by three separate filtered datasets working together. Each level in the chain gets its own dataset, and the actual filtering logic lives on that dataset's Filters tab: Expression, Operator, and a Value that's a reference to the parameter chosen one level up, like [@CountryParameter]. So the State dataset's query returns every state, but its Filters tab narrows that down to just the states belonging to whichever country was picked. The ordering requirement trips people up constantly -- the order under the Parameters node in the Report Data pane is literally the order the reader gets prompted, and since the State dataset's filter depends on knowing the Country parameter's value already, Country has to come first in that list, or the report tries to filter on a parameter the reader hasn't answered yet.

questions.title: What makes a subscription 'data-driven'
questions.prompt: Explain what distinguishes a data-driven subscription from a standard subscription in SSRS, and what two things the subscription's query result set actually controls.
questions.modelAnswer: A standard subscription has one fixed set of delivery settings. A data-driven subscription instead queries a subscriber database each time it runs, and uses whatever comes back to determine the recipients, the delivery settings, and the report parameter values for that run -- the mechanism to use when who gets a report, or what parameters they see it with, changes over time and shouldn't require manually editing a subscription every time it does. This requires defining a dataset (a data source plus a query) before the subscription can be built at all. Two facts about that query's result set matter more than anything else: columns determine what you're allowed to map to delivery settings and parameters (an email subscription needs a column of email addresses), and rows determine how many deliveries get generated -- ten thousand rows means ten thousand separate deliveries, one per row.
questions.professionalAnswer: The simplest way I'd put it: a standard subscription is baked-in and static -- same recipient, same settings, every time it fires. A data-driven subscription instead runs a query against a subscriber database at execution time and builds the delivery list fresh, every single run, from whatever that query returns. That's the right tool whenever the recipient list or the parameter values genuinely change over time -- think a report that needs to go to whichever regional manager owns a territory this month, without anyone manually touching the subscription. The two things I'd emphasize about the query results: columns decide what you're even allowed to map to delivery fields -- no email column means you can't map an email field -- and rows decide volume, literally one delivery per row, so a 10,000-row query produces 10,000 separate deliveries. Before I'd ever paste a query into the subscription wizard, I'd run it in SSMS first and sanity-check both the columns and the row count, because debugging it inside the wizard's query-timeout window is painful.

questions.title: A data-driven subscription sent the wrong number of emails
questions.prompt: A data-driven subscription was supposed to send one report to each of 40 regional managers, but it actually generated 120 deliveries. What would you check first, and what's the most likely explanation?
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing to check is the subscription's underlying query, run directly in SQL Server Management Studio -- because rows in that result set directly determine how many deliveries get generated, one per row. If 120 deliveries went out instead of the expected 40, the query is almost certainly returning 120 rows, not 40 -- most likely because of a join that fans out (e.g. joining managers to a table where each manager has multiple records, like one row per territory or one row per month, producing three rows per manager instead of one). The fix is to correct the query so it returns exactly one row per intended recipient -- often by aggregating, deduplicating, or tightening the join -- rather than trying to fix anything inside the subscription wizard itself, since the wizard only consumes whatever rows the query hands it.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always to pull the subscription's query out and run it directly in SSMS, because the wizard is just a dumb consumer of whatever rows that query returns -- one delivery per row, no exceptions. 120 deliveries for 40 intended recipients is a strong signal the query is returning 3 rows per manager instead of 1, and the most common cause I'd look for is a join that fans out -- maybe the query joins managers to a territories or monthly-summary table where each manager legitimately has three related rows, and nobody deduplicated or aggregated before handing that result to the subscription. Once I confirm the row count problem in SSMS, the fix is entirely in the query -- tightening the join, adding a DISTINCT, or aggregating down to one row per manager -- not anything inside the subscription wizard itself, which has no logic of its own to blame here.

Assuming the delivery count is unrelated to the query's row count
Not testing the query independently in SSMS before re-examining the wizard configuration
Fixing it by manually limiting deliveries rather than correcting the row-level root cause in the query
keyPoints: Delivery count always equals the query's row count -- one delivery per row
A 3x delivery count strongly suggests a fan-out join producing multiple rows per intended recipient
Diagnose by running the query directly in SSMS, outside the subscription wizard
The fix belongs in the query (dedup/aggregate/tighten join), not in the subscription wizard

questions.title: Nested groups and interactive sort in the Grouping pane
questions.prompt: You need a tablix grouped by Category, with Subcategory nested under it, and you want report viewers to be able to click a column header to re-sort the detail rows by price at runtime. Describe how you'd set this up using the Grouping pane and Interactive Sorting.
questions.modelAnswer: In the Grouping pane's Row Groups section, drag Category in first to create the parent group, then drag Subcategory underneath it (not beside it) so it becomes a child group, nested and indented under Category -- a child group repeats once per parent instance, which is exactly the Category-then-Subcategory hierarchy needed. This is a fixed, design-time grouping structure, separate from sorting. To let viewers re-sort the detail rows by price at runtime, right-click the price column's text box, choose Text Box Properties, go to Interactive Sorting, check 'Enable interactive sorting on this text box,' choose 'Detail rows' (not Groups), and set 'Sort by' to the price field. This adds a clickable header button without touching the report's fixed design-time sort order, and the two can coexist -- a sensible default order plus a runtime override per column.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build the grouping first, independent of sorting, because they're genuinely separate concerns even though people often conflate them. In the Grouping pane's Row Groups, I drag Category down first -- that's the parent. Then I drag Subcategory underneath Category specifically, not beside it, which is what makes it a child rather than a sibling -- the visual cue is the indentation, and functionally a child group repeats once per parent instance, which is exactly the nested hierarchy I want. One practical tip I always mention: when dragging fields into the Grouping pane, I'm careful not to drag across other report items on the design surface, since that can accidentally select those items and deselect the data region I'm working on. For the interactive sort, that's a completely separate step on the price column specifically -- right-click its text box, Text Box Properties, Interactive Sorting tab, check the enable box, choose Detail rows since I want to sort the actual data rows rather than the groups, and point Sort by at the price field. That gives viewers a clickable header without changing the report's own default sort order underneath it.

Choosing 'Groups' instead of 'Detail rows' in Interactive Sorting when the intent is to sort the actual data rows
Dragging a field across other report items on the design surface, accidentally deselecting the intended data region

questions.title: A cascading parameter chain throws an error at runtime
questions.prompt: A report with Country, State, and City cascading parameters throws an error the moment it's opened, before the reader has selected anything. A colleague says they just added the three parameters and their dataset filters but didn't check the order in the Parameters node. Diagnose the likely cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is exactly the thing the colleague flagged: the order parameters appear under the Parameters node in the Report Data pane determines the order the reader is prompted for them, and that order has to match the dependency chain -- Country before State before City. If State (or its dataset's query) ends up evaluated before Country has a value, its filter is trying to reference [@CountryParameter] before that parameter has been set, which produces an error immediately rather than waiting for the reader to interact with anything. The fix is to reorder the parameters in the Report Data pane's Parameters node so Country comes first, State second, City third, matching the actual dependency chain each dataset's Filters tab relies on.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given that the colleague already flagged they skipped checking the parameter order, that's exactly where I'd look first, because this is the single most common cause of a cascading parameter chain failing immediately rather than waiting for reader interaction. Each dataset's Filters tab in a cascading chain references the parameter one level up -- State's filter references [@CountryParameter], City's references [@StateParameter]. If the Parameters node in the Report Data pane doesn't list them in that same dependency order, the report can try to evaluate a dataset's filter against a parameter that hasn't been given a value yet, which throws an error right at open time instead of gracefully prompting step by step. The fix is mechanical: open the Parameters node, confirm Country sits above State, and State sits above City, reordering them if they don't.

Not realizing an error at report-open time (vs. after a selection) is itself a strong clue pointing at ordering
Fixing it by removing the cascading filters instead of simply reordering the Parameters node
Confusing the fix for this with Allow multiple values settings, which is unrelated

An error at open time (before any selection) is a strong signal of an ordering problem
Each dataset's filter references the parameter one level up, which must already have a value
The fix is reordering the Parameters node, not touching the filter logic itself

questions.title: Explaining a report change timeline to a non-technical stakeholder
questions.prompt: A sales manager asks why adding one more parameter to an existing SSRS report -- 'just let me filter by region too' -- is going to take more than a quick five-minute change. How would you explain this to someone with no technical background?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer translates the technical reality into terms the stakeholder cares about without being condescending: explain that a new parameter isn't just a dropdown on the screen -- it usually means changing the underlying dataset's query to accept and filter by the new value, checking whether any existing parameters need to cascade from or into the new one, re-testing the report with real data to make sure nothing else broke, and in some cases updating any subscriptions or other reports that share the same dataset. Framing it concretely -- 'it's less like flipping a switch and more like adding a new ingredient to a recipe that's already being served to other tables' -- helps non-technical stakeholders understand why 'just one filter' touches more than the screen they're looking at, while still giving them a realistic timeline instead of a vague 'it's complicated.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd avoid jargon entirely and anchor the explanation in what they already understand: the report they see is the last step in a chain, and changing what they see usually means changing something earlier in that chain too. Adding a region filter isn't just adding a box on the screen -- it means going back to where the report gets its data and teaching that query how to filter by region, then checking whether region needs to interact with any filters that already exist (does picking a region change what shows up in another dropdown?), then actually testing it with real data to make sure the numbers still add up correctly, not just that the dropdown appears. I'd give them a concrete estimate rather than just 'it's complicated' -- something like 'I can have this ready and tested by Thursday' -- because non-technical stakeholders generally don't need the mechanics, they need to know it's being handled and roughly when.

Not giving any concrete timeline, leaving the stakeholder with only 'it's complicated'
Over-explaining every technical step instead of focusing on what the stakeholder actually needs to know

questions.title: What CALCULATE actually does
questions.prompt: Explain what the DAX CALCULATE function does, in one sentence, and then explain what happens by default when CALCULATE's filter argument targets a column that already has an active filter from a slicer.
questions.modelAnswer: CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside a modified filter context -- that's the whole function in one sentence, but nearly everything advanced in DAX is built on top of it. Its syntax is CALCULATE(<expression>, <filter1>, <filter2>, ...), where the expression is almost always a measure or an aggregation, and the filters narrow or change the filter context it's evaluated in. When a filter argument targets a column that isn't already filtered, the new filter is simply added. When the column is already filtered -- say, by a slicer -- CALCULATE's filter overwrites the existing one by default, rather than combining with it. This overwrite behavior is intentional: it's what lets you force an expression to ignore what a user selected and substitute your own condition instead.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain CALCULATE as the function that changes the rules an expression is evaluated under -- everything else in DAX that feels 'advanced,' from time intelligence to percent-of-total, is really just CALCULATE with a particular kind of filter passed into it. The syntax is simple: an expression first, then any number of filter arguments. The behavior that trips people up is what happens when a filter argument targets a column that's already filtered elsewhere, like a slicer on the report page. By default, CALCULATE doesn't combine with that existing filter -- it overwrites it entirely for that one expression. So if I write Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue"), and the report page already has a slicer set to 'Red,' that measure still shows blue-only revenue, because my CALCULATE filter replaced the slicer's filter rather than intersecting with it. That's deliberate and powerful -- but it's also the single most common source of 'why is my measure ignoring the slicer' confusion, which is exactly why KEEPFILTERS exists for the cases where you want the opposite behavior.
questions.example:
Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue")
-- Even with a report-level slicer on Product[Color] set to "Red",
-- this measure still returns blue-only revenue, because CALCULATE's
-- filter overwrites the slicer's filter on that same column by default.
commonMistakes: Describing CALCULATE only as 'a SUM with a filter' instead of the general filter-context-modification mechanism it is
Assuming a CALCULATE filter always combines with existing filters instead of overwriting them by default
Forgetting the filter argument can be a Boolean expression, a table expression (FILTER), or a filter modifier function
Not recognizing that time-intelligence functions and percent-of-total patterns are just CALCULATE under the hood
keyPoints: CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside a modified filter context
The filter argument can be a simple condition, a table expression, or a filter modifier
By default, a CALCULATE filter overwrites an existing filter on the same column, not combines with it
This overwrite behavior is what makes CALCULATE powerful for overriding user selections

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a correct one-sentence definition of CALCULATE
Correctly explains the default overwrite behavior on an already-filtered column
Provides a correct, relevant example

questions.title: Writing a percent-of-total measure
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure that shows each product category's sales as a percentage of total sales across the whole table, regardless of what category filter is currently applied on the report page.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the classic percent-of-total pattern, built with DIVIDE and REMOVEFILTERS. The numerator respects whatever's currently filtered (one category, if that's what's selected). The denominator wraps the same total-sales expression in CALCULATE with REMOVEFILTERS() as the filter argument, which strips away every active filter, giving the grand total across the entire table regardless of what's selected. Dividing the filtered numerator by the unfiltered denominator produces each row's share of the whole.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as two layers. First, I already have (or create) a plain Total Sales measure that just does SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) and naturally respects whatever filter context it's placed in -- one category if that's what the visual is sliced by. Then the percent-of-total measure wraps that same aggregation twice: once left alone as the numerator, and once inside CALCULATE with REMOVEFILTERS() as the denominator, which strips away every filter and gives me the grand total no matter what's selected. I always use DIVIDE instead of a plain '/' operator, specifically because DIVIDE handles a zero denominator gracefully instead of throwing a divide-by-zero error, which matters the moment someone filters down to a category with literally zero total sales in it.
questions.example:
%Sales =
DIVIDE(
    [Total Sales],
    CALCULATE([Total Sales], REMOVEFILTERS())
)
-- Numerator respects the current filter (e.g. one category);
-- denominator strips all filters via REMOVEFILTERS(), giving the grand total.
-- DIVIDE avoids a divide-by-zero error if the filtered total is 0.
commonMistakes: Using a plain '/' operator instead of DIVIDE, risking a divide-by-zero error
Forgetting to wrap REMOVEFILTERS() inside CALCULATE -- it only has an effect as a CALCULATE filter argument
Using ALL() instead of REMOVEFILTERS() without understanding the subtle scoping differences between them
Computing the denominator from a hardcoded total instead of dynamically removing filters, breaking if the data changes
keyPoints: REMOVEFILTERS() inside CALCULATE strips all active filters for the grand total
The numerator is left as a plain measure so it respects the current filter context
DIVIDE is preferred over '/' because it handles a zero denominator gracefully
This pattern generalizes to any percent-of-total calculation

Correctly leaves the numerator respecting the current filter context
